papers.title: Geometry-Conditioned Hyperalignment for Generalizable EEG Decoding Across Datasets and Paradigms
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) supports promising applications, but daily use remains limited by poor cross-subject and cross-dataset generalisation. That is because EEG recordings made with different electrode montages do not even share an observation space, and each subjects's leadfield projects the same neural sources onto the scalp differently. We present hTSMNet, which combines a novel geometry-conditioned hyperalignment frontend with a Riemannian symmetric positive-definite (SPD) manifold backbone that reduces the residual cross-subject distribution shift. From electrode coordinates alone, the frontend builds a linear map from any montage onto a fixed set of scalp anchors, placing every recording in one shared space. Because this map has no subjectspecific parameters, an unseen subject, dataset, or montage is aligned from its geometry alone, so transfer is zero-shot by construction. On a leave-one-dataset-out left-/right-hand motor-imagery (MI) benchmark across three datasets (172 subjects) and eight comparators, hTSMNet matches the strongest comparator at strict zero-shot, and attains the highest accuracy on every dataset once a few calibration trials for adjusting only final-layer classifier are available. We show that it orients the binary decision the same way in every dataset, so that a single linear rule learned on the source data is already correctly oriented on a held-out one. The same frozen MI-pretrained model also transfers across paradigms: with only a re-fit final-layer classifier, hTSMNet decodes mental workload and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) well above chance, yet remains at chance on stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERP). This dissociation follows from the architecture: covariance pooling reads oscillatory band power and is largely insensitive to the phase-locked potentials that ERP tasks depend on. What the representation generalizes is a signal family (band-limited oscillatory activity), not the named task. Geometry-conditioned hyperalignment thus yields an inspectable representation, which is generalizable across datasets and, within the oscillatory regime, across paradigms.

ai.reason: Zero-shot geometry-conditioned alignment across montages and subjects directly addresses signal normalization and small-calibration transfer, highly relevant to adapting models across recording systems and animals.
ai.summary: Introduces hTSMNet, combining geometry-conditioned hyperalignment, which maps any electrode montage onto fixed scalp anchors using coordinates alone, with an SPD manifold backbone for zero-shot cross-subject and cross-dataset EEG decoding. On a leave-one-dataset-out motor-imagery benchmark across three datasets (172 subjects), it matched the strongest zero-shot comparator and achieved the highest accuracy on every dataset after minimal classifier-only calibration; the frozen model also transferred to mental workload and SSVEP but not stimulus-locked ERP, indicating generalization of band-limited oscillatory representations rather than named tasks.

papers.title: Temporal-context learning for subject-independent sleep staging with non-contact multi-frequency radar.
papers.abstract: Contactless radar may support unobtrusive sleep monitoring, but reliable five-stage evaluation requires participant-isolated testing and a clear assessment of the contribution of model components. The analysis included all 32 overnight recordings (33 964 labelled 30 s epochs) in the PhysioNet Sleep Bioradiolocation Database. Eight documented I/Q channel pairs spanning 3.6-4.0 GHz underwent complex clutter suppression, phase demodulation, fixed 0.05-0.70 Hz zero-phase filtering and resampling to 10 Hz. A 266 342-parameter composite network combined a shared one-dimensional encoder, cross-frequency contrastive initialization, quality-conditioned frequency fusion and a bidirectional gated recurrent unit over nine epochs. Eight deterministic folds each used 24 training, four validation and four held-out test participants, so every participant was tested once. Primary outcomes were participant-level five-stage macro-F1, balanced accuracy and Cohen's kappa. The full network achieved accuracy 0.434, macro-F1 0.376 (95% confidence interval 0.344-0.409), balanced accuracy 0.432 (0.405-0.457) and kappa 0.271 (0.235-0.308). Removing temporal context reduced macro-F1 by 0.072 (0.050-0.095), whereas neither contrastive initialization nor learned fusion showed an incremental held-out benefit. An independently trained early-fusion CNN-BiGRU achieved macro-F1 0.296. The participant-isolated evaluation identifies temporal context as the main contributor among the assessed components and provides a reproducible reference for future radar-based sleep-staging studies.

ai.reason: Directly targets five-stage sleep staging with participant-isolated evaluation and component ablations; strong sleep-classification methodology transferable despite radar modality.
ai.summary: Developed a temporal-context learning model for subject-independent sleep staging using non-contact multi-frequency radar, achieving macro-F1 of 0.376 on held-out participants. Removing temporal context reduced macro-F1 by 0.072, identifying it as the main contributor among assessed components.

papers.title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

papers.title: Multi-day recalibration-free electrophysiology interface based on carbon nanotube thin film dry electrodes.
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological signals provide crucial and reliable information for decoding behavioral and cognitive human states. However, existing electrode interfaces are susceptible to artifacts or drift over time, thereby requiring frequent machine-learning model retraining. Here we present an end-to-end design of dry electrodes based on carbon nanotube (CNT) thin films, synthesized by a roll-to-roll floating catalyst chemical vapor deposition process. By balancing structural and electrical properties, we achieved low electrode-skin impedance, high signal fidelity, minimal motion artifacts, high breathability, and biocompatibility, outperforming the gold standard wet electrodes. In a multichannel myoelectric interface demonstration, these CNT electrodes maintained stable signals and consistent task performance across 14 days using only minutes of training data and no further model retraining. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a multi-day recalibration-free dry electrode system under naturalistic conditions, achieved by stable electrode-skin interface, rather than ongoing algorithmic adaptation.

ai.reason: Addresses signal stability, drift, and multi-day calibration-free decoding with short training data, relevant to normalization across recording systems and user calibration.
ai.summary: Presented carbon nanotube thin-film dry electrodes synthesized via roll-to-roll floating catalyst CVD that achieved low impedance and high signal fidelity, outperforming wet electrodes. In a multichannel myoelectric interface, stable signals and task performance were maintained across 14 days without model retraining.

papers.title: Macroscale dynamics of EEG microstates constitute the periodic and aperiodic features of the neural power spectrum
papers.abstract: The global signal characteristics of scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) are composed of periodic oscillatory rhythms and aperiodic broadband fluctuations that together comprise the neural power spectrum. Spectral decomposition of these features has long served as the primary window into the macroscale characteristics of human brain activity. Here, we propose that the primary periodic rhythms and majority share of broadband spectral power within the brain's dominant frequencies are the frequency-domain representations of the dynamics of EEG microstates. Microstates are characterized by a small repertoire of topographic voltage configurations that each reflect the momentary functional state of the cortex, and it is their time-domain dynamics that mathematically constitute periodic and aperiodic spectral features. We isolated and removed the spatial projections of distinct microstate configurations from high-density EEG using orthogonal subspace projection applied to both the surface scalp recordings and their modeled cortical generators to computationally test this dependency. Spectral parameterization of the residual power spectral density revealed that removing these spatial projections strongly attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and features of the aperiodic 1/f background. Selectively removing specific microstate configurations also demonstrated that each configuration aligned with spatially specific oscillatory and aperiodic 1/f components. Furthermore, correlational analyses of microstate temporal dynamics demonstrated that the average duration and temporal persistence of microstates strongly correlate with periodic alpha power, theta power, and the aperiodic 1/f background. Our findings suggest that dominant periodic and aperiodic spectral features are more accurately understood as the frequency-domain expressions of the dynamics of EEG microstates.

ai.reason: Links microstate dynamics to periodic/aperiodic spectral features using subspace projection and spectral parameterization, an interpretable time-frequency/aperiodic analytic framework potentially transferable to sleep spectral analysis.
ai.summary: Used orthogonal subspace projection to remove spatial projections of distinct EEG microstate configurations from high-density scalp recordings and modeled cortical generators, then spectrally parameterized the residual power. Removing these projections attenuated alpha and theta rhythms and the aperiodic 1/f background in configuration-specific ways, and microstate duration and temporal persistence correlated strongly with periodic alpha, theta, and 1/f features, supporting microstate dynamics as the time-domain source of periodic and aperiodic spectra.

papers.title: Different Pipelines, Different EEG Microstate Results: Evidence from Dementia Samples.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) microstate analysis has been proposed as a potential biomarker for neurological disorders, yet the influence of analytic pipeline choices on clinical findings remains unclear. Resting-state EEG from patients with Alzheimer's disease (n = 36), frontotemporal dementia (n = 23), and healthy controls (n = 29) was analyzed using multiple microstate pipelines combining k-means or atomize-agglomerate hierarchical clustering with different temporal-smoothing conditions. Bayesian ANCOVA showed that evidence for group differences varied substantially across pipelines, particularly as a function of temporal smoothing. Rank-correlation analyses further demonstrated reduced agreement between smoothed and unsmoothed pipelines, indicating that smoothing altered the relative ordering of microstate temporal parameters across participants. To assess methodological stability, intra-subject split-half analyses were performed. Microstate topographies showed > 92% shared variance between independent data halves, whereas the reliability of duration, occurrence, and coverage varied across pipelines. Unsmoothed pipelines generally showed equal or greater split-half reliability for selected microstate B measures, and the reproducibility of clinical effect sizes differed by clustering algorithm and diagnostic contrast. These findings demonstrate that temporal smoothing and clustering choices can substantially influence the reliability and clinical interpretation of EEG microstate measures, underscoring the need for explicit pipeline validation in biomarker studies.

ai.reason: Directly examines how analytic pipeline choices change EEG microstate results and reliability, valuable for reproducible, cross-dataset method design.
ai.summary: Analyzed resting-state EEG from Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and healthy controls using multiple microstate pipelines, showing that evidence for group differences varied substantially with temporal smoothing and clustering algorithm. Split-half reliability of microstate measures also differed across pipelines, highlighting the need for explicit pipeline validation.

papers.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes
papers.abstract: Early and accurate identification of neurodegenerative disorders has notable implications for treatment and quality of life. Whereas neuroimaging-based biomarkers can accurately identify neurodegenerative subtypes, EEG represents a low-cost alternative that could expand access to dementia care. Here, we investigated whether six data-driven EEG latent factors, derived by nonnegative tensor decomposition of clinical EEGs, differ systematically across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative phenotypes. In 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET acquired within one year of each other, factor expression was compared across 14 diagnostic classes assigned by StateViewer, a validated artificial intelligence framework for FDG-PET interpretation. To separate disease-general severity from phenotype-specific topography, each factor was also regressed on a subject-level slowing index. Finally, we related the factors to regional FDG uptake and to neuropsychological performance (n = 98) and assessed their potential utility for single-subject classification. Four factors reflecting neurophysiological oscillations (posterior alpha, Rolandic beta, frontotemporal delta-theta and posterior theta-slow alpha) varied significantly across phenotypes, with attenuation of faster and augmentation of slower rhythms most pronounced in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), dysexecutive Alzheimer disease (AD) and posterior cortical atrophy, whereas factors dominated by eye-movement and muscle artifact showed no robust phenotypic association. Alpha and beta effects were largely attributable to overall slowing, whereas posterior theta-slow alpha became more phenotype-specific after adjustment (eta-squared 0.082 to 0.147), dissociating the Alzheimer disease spectrum from frontotemporal syndromes. The slowing index tracked with an FDG-PET pattern highly associated with DLB across the cohort, irrespective of assigned phenotype (r = 0.51, P < 0.001). Consistent with a model in which dementia phenotypes reflect altered hippocampal-neocortical oscillatory coupling (stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion), frontotemporal delta-theta tracked a limbocortical axis of metabolic pattern expression, rising with neocortical and falling with limbic-predominant involvement, independent of overall slowing and phenotype. Each factor mapped onto a distinct metabolic topography, with frontotemporal delta-theta resembling Alzheimer-type hypometabolism and posterior theta-slow alpha the medial occipital hypometabolism of DLB. In terms of neuropsychological performance, Rolandic beta was associated with executive functions, and frontotemporal delta-theta with memory, visuospatial and global performance. Using these four factors alone, an exploratory logistic regression classifier separated cognitively unimpaired participants from DLB, posterior cortical atrophy, typical AD, and dysexecutive AD (area under the curve > 0.8) but poorly discriminated frontotemporal dementia phenotypes canonically associated with 4-repeat tau. Thus, data-driven decomposition of clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artifact into factors that track metabolic phenotype, regional metabolism and cognition, capturing both overall slowing and phenotype-specific patterns. This work informs the further development of scalable, biology-informed EEG-based phenotyping of neurodegenerative disease.

A slowing index tracked a DLB-associated metabolic pattern, and the factors supported exploratory classification of dementia phenotypes with AUC > 0.8 for several contrasts.

papers.title: Detection of linear dependencies in EEG oscillatory sources via PARALIND and block-term decomposition: A comparative study.
papers.abstract: Narrowband oscillatory rhythms in electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are fundamental signatures of neural dynamics, crucial for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and monitoring neurological disorders. While traditionally detected and analyzed via Independent or Principal Component Analysis in the time-space domain, tensor decomposition in the time-space-frequency domain offers superior resolution. The CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) model is widely used for this purpose due to itssimplicity and interpretability. However, it often fails to resolve rhythms or requires excessive components when source collinearity exists (i.e., a situation where oscillatory rhythms share characteristics across temporal, spatial, or frequency modes), leading to instability and increased computational complexity.Approach: This study evaluates two alternative tensor decomposition models - Parallel Profiles with Linear Dependencies (PARALIND) and Block-Term Decomposition (BTD) - which explicitly accommodate linear dependencies among latent components. We compared these models against CP using simulated EEG data with known ground-truth structures and real-world recordings.Main results: PARALIND and BTD achieved interpretability comparable to CP while providing more stable factor estimates at moderate noise levels in simulated data, although both models struggled to identify the true latent structure under challenging conditions. Overall, when their modelling assumptions were satisfied, PARALIND and BTD successfully disentangled complex, overlapping neural sources that CP struggled to isolate. In real data, both models recovered a latent structure similar to that identified by CP, but with fewer loadings. Following the principle of parsimony, PARALIND and BTD may therefore be preferable in this setting.Significance: By overcoming the collinearity limitations inherent in CP decomposition, these findings establish a more reliable framework for neurophysiologically interpretable tensor decomposition of EEG signals. While clinical translation was not evaluated in this work, this methodological advance provides a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing BCI stability and investigating biomarkers of neurological conditions.

ai.reason: Compares CP, PARALIND, and BTD for resolving collinear oscillatory sources; a transferable spectral/time-space-frequency method relevant to interpretable feature extraction.
ai.summary: Compared PARALIND and block-term decomposition against CANDECOMP/PARAFAC for detecting linear dependencies in EEG oscillatory sources using simulated and real data. PARALIND and BTD provided more stable factor estimates at moderate noise and disentangled overlapping sources that CP struggled to isolate, with fewer loadings in real data.

papers.title: Interictal Electroencephalographic Characteristics of the Human Centromedian Thalamic Nucleus Recorded in Focal Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: The centromedian (CM) thalamic nucleus is critical in sleep-wake regulation and epileptic networks; yet its electroencephalography (EEG) characteristics remain incompletely understood. CM EEG across vigilance states and interictal epileptic discharges (IEDs) in focal epilepsy were investigated. Interictal stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recordings from the CM and neighboring ventroposterior (VP) and ventrolateral (VL) nuclei were analyzed with synchronous cortical SEEG and scalp EEG during wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement sleep, rapid eye movement sleep, and spontaneous non-epileptic arousal. Spectral power was quantified across frequency bands. Sleep-related thalamic activities and thalamic IEDs were visually identified. SEEG data from 33 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and 3 non-epileptic individuals were analyzed. CM exhibited continuous fast activity during wakefulness and delta/theta-dominant activity during sleep, confirmed by increased gamma-fast ripple power in wakefulness and enhanced delta/theta power in sleep (all p < 0.014). During spontaneous non-epileptic arousal, thalamic EEG changes preceded scalp EEG arousal (median 800 ms; interquartile range: 400-1500 ms). Four sleep-related thalamic EEG activities were reproducibly observed in non-epileptic individuals, supporting a potential physiological nature. Thalamic IEDs occurred in 36.4% of patients with focal epilepsy, invariably involved the CM. Thalamic IEDs were more frequent in extratemporal than temporal lobe epilepsy and were not associated with surgical outcome. CM SEEG demonstrates distinct, state-dependent electrophysiological dynamics across the sleep-wake cycle and preferential involvement in interictal epileptic activity compared with VL/VP nuclei. These findings lay the foundation for a thalamic EEG atlas and refine understanding of differential engagement of thalamic nuclei in epileptic networks.

Thalamic interictal epileptic discharges occurred in 36.4% of patients, invariably involving the CM, more often in extratemporal than temporal lobe epilepsy and not associated with surgical outcome.

papers.title: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
papers.abstract: Gastric interoceptive attention to internal, bodily signals such as hunger, satiety, and fullness are important for regulating feeding behaviors. However, abnormal processing or sensitivity to these can lead to disorders that result in overly restrictive or excessive consumption, highlighting the need for better understanding of the cortical processing of these cues. Specifically, understanding cortical representations of self-perceived gastric fullness have yet to be studied in humans. In this work, we demonstrate that consistently across individuals, the broadband power spectral density of EEG signals, as quantified by the aperiodic exponent, flattens after individuals drink water until fullness. Simultaneous measures of the stomach and heart demonstrate increased vagal drive to peripheral organs. We further find that changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns are associated with changes in the frequency of gastric oscillations. Overall, this suggests that the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker for assessing gastric interoceptive attention.

ai.summary: Showed that the EEG aperiodic exponent flattens after water intake to fullness consistently across individuals, accompanied by increased vagal drive to peripheral organs measured via simultaneous gastric and cardiac recordings. Changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns were associated with changes in gastric oscillation frequency, suggesting the exponent as a noninvasive biomarker of gastric interoceptive attention.

papers.title: Talking Brains: Neonatal Aperiodic Activity in Resting State EEG Relates to Later Communicative Abilities
papers.abstract: Communicative abilities acquired over the first year of life are foundational for language development. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying these abilities can explain individual differences and improve predictions of later language outcomes. While prior research on neural markers of language development has focused predominantly on oscillatory neural activity, the underlying aperiodic component of the neural signal may provide further insights into cortical maturation by indirectly reflecting variation in neural excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance. In neurodevelopmental conditions, both reduced and elevated aperiodic activity are linked to atypical development, and initial evidence from at-risk cohorts also relates aperiodic activity to language outcome. Moving beyond clinical populations, the present study examined whether aperiodic activity during neonatal resting-state EEG relates to 12-month communicative abilities in typically developing infants. Aperiodic offset and exponent were extracted from resting-state EEG recorded two weeks after birth in n = 50 neonates using the FOOOF algorithm. At 12 months, communicative abilities were assessed with the parent-report CSBS-DP Infant-Toddler Checklist. Quadratic regression analyses showed an inverted U-shaped relationship between the neonatal aperiodic exponent and communicative abilities: both lower and higher exponent values were associated with poorer outcomes, with intermediate values linked to better abilities. No robust association was found for the offset. These findings suggest that aperiodic activity captures variability in early communicative development, with an optimum at intermediate levels, consistent with a balanced E/I state. The scope of aperiodic brain activity as a developmental marker may thus extend beyond clinical populations to predicting communicative development in healthy infants.

Quadratic regression showed an inverted U-shaped relationship between the neonatal aperiodic exponent and later communicative abilities, with both lower and higher exponent values associated with poorer outcomes and intermediate values with better abilities.

papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result
papers.abstract: Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. We asked how much short-horizon warning survives a pre-specified, locked evaluation. Continuous video-EEG from 21 monitored children (1315 h) formed the development cohort. A statistical-process-control warning method, evaluated under a written protocol, detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. We re-designed it as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, froze it with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, and estimated its performance by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation: 15 of 45 seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. Applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database; 101 evaluable seizures), the frozen scheme detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. Scalp-EEG warning should be evaluated under pre-specified rules against structured chance levels; the frozen scheme and framework are offered as a reference.

papers.title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
papers.abstract: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To overcome these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients, we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves preprocessing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

The combination of SelectKBest, SVM, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieved the highest accuracy at 72%, outperforming the other methods.

papers.title: In-ear electroencephalography: a systematic review of technology, applications, challenges, and future directions.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to monitor brain activity in both clinical and research settings. However, conventional scalp EEG systems require multiple electrodes, specialised equipment, and trained personnel, which limits their practicality for long-term monitoring in everyday environments. In-ear EEG has emerged as a promising wearable alternative that enables discreet and portable neural monitoring. This systematic review examines the current state of research on in-ear EEG technologies. Twenty-four studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed thematically. The literature highlights rapid progress in device miniaturisation and wearable design, with reported applications including sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive workload assessment, fatigue monitoring, and emotion recognition. Despite these advances, challenges remain related to signal quality, spatial coverage, and motion artefacts. Further research is required to validate in-ear EEG for broader clinical and real-world applications.

ai.reason: Reviews portable in-ear EEG hardware including sleep monitoring and artifacts, adjacent to long-term recording needs but not an algorithmic method.
ai.summary: Systematically reviewed 24 studies on in-ear (ear-EEG) technologies, documenting progress in device miniaturization and wearable design with applications in sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive workload, fatigue monitoring, and emotion recognition. Remaining challenges include signal quality, spatial coverage, and motion artifacts, requiring further validation for broader clinical and real-world use.

papers.title: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil--brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
papers.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil--brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. We therefore asked whether the spectrotemporal and directional organization of such coupling can be captured with wearable systems to test their use in naturalistic settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting-state pupil--brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Cross-correlation, mutual information, and Granger causality analyses revealed that pupil--brain coupling displayed clear frequency-dependent organization. Lower EEG frequencies (2-12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger-causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG-to-pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Overall, these findings align well and extend previous evidence on spontaneous pupil--brain coupling, demonstrating that lightweight and movable wearable devices are suitable to characterize spectrotemporal and directional pupil--brain interactions. In turn, these results encourage future fundamental and translational research in naturalistic environments.

ai.summary: Used wearable mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) to test whether spectrotemporal and directional pupil-brain coupling is detectable in naturalistic, continuous resting-state recordings with interoceptive attention. papers.title: Stimulated human cortical waves: spatiotemporal dynamics across development
papers.abstract: Traveling waves of neural activity are fundamental to cortical function, yet their spatiotemporal dynamics and structural constraints remain less understood in human brain. Conventional analyses focus on network topology and spatial geometry of neural signals, with limited emphasis on wave dynamics at high spatiotemporal resolutions. Here, we applied a manifold-based optical flow algorithm to an open-access intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) dataset from the single-pulse stimulation cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) paradigm, enabling direct construction of high-temporal-resolution cortical neural activity velocity fields. Spatiotemporal mode decomposition revealed a hierarchical organization: large-scale plane waves (mediating global propagation) dominate, complemented by local patterns for local computation. Dominant plane wave directions correlate with underlying white matter fibre tract orientations, indicating anatomical guidance of cortical dynamics. Velocity field singular points (sources, sinks, spirals and saddles) are non-randomly distributed, associating with default mode network (DMN) hubs. We further identified a nonlinear relationship between cortical wave speed and age, with developmental phases paralleling white matter maturation and aging. Our findings link cortical wave dynamics to anatomy, functional networks, and neurodevelopment, establishing wave speed as a potential yet important biomarker for brain function and health.

ai.reason: Applies manifold-based optical flow and mode decomposition to iEEG dynamics; methodologically interesting but high-density intracranial and not directly sleep/EEG-transferable.
ai.summary: Applied a manifold-based optical flow algorithm to intracranial EEG cortico-cortical evoked potentials from single-pulse stimulation to reconstruct high-temporal-resolution cortical velocity fields, revealing hierarchical organization dominated by large-scale plane waves plus local patterns. Dominant plane wave directions aligned with white matter fiber tract orientation, velocity field singular points associated with default mode network hubs, and cortical wave speed showed a nonlinear relationship with age paralleling white matter maturation and aging.

papers.title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.

papers.title: Multimodal EEG-fNIRS complexity analysis can reveal the neurovascular coupling change with aging.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate age-related changes in neurovascular coupling (NVC) function of the brain using a multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) approach combined with nonlinear entropy analysis. The study included 20 young adults and 20 older adults. We simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS data during four cognitive tasks (auditory attention task, verbal fluency task, upper limb motor task, and recognition memory task). We calculated sample entropy (SampEn) and conditional entropy (CondEn) for five EEG frequency sub-bands (Delta: 1-4 Hz, Theta: 4-8 Hz, Alpha: 8-12 Hz, Beta: 12-30 Hz, Gamma: 30-40 Hz) as well as for fNIRS signals (oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin, HbO and HbR) to quantify neural and hemodynamic complexity of brain activity. Additionally, cross-sample entropy (Cross-SampEn) and cross-conditional entropy (Cross-CondEn) between EEG and fNIRS signals were computed to evaluate NVC function. Group differences were assessed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with age group as the fixed factor and sex and years of education as covariates. Older adults showed higher EEG SampEn or CondEn in selected frequency bands during the auditory attention task and the encoding and recognition phases of the recognition memory task. For fNIRS, older adults showed lower HbO SampEn during memory recognition. Cross-modal analysis showed lower beta-HbR Cross-SampEn during the left upper limb motor task and higher theta-HbR Cross-SampEn during memory encoding in older adults. Aging is associated with task-specific alterations in neural complexity, hemodynamic complexity, and the cross-modal temporal relationship between EEG and fNIRS signals. These findings suggest that age-related changes in NVC-related dynamics are better characterized as dynamic reorganization rather than a uniform enhancement or impairment, and support the potential of multimodal entropy analysis for characterizing age-related neurovascular coupling change.

papers.title: A collaborative network of bi-Mamba and CAFS for multi-task classification of unilateral lower limb.
papers.abstract: Accurate decoding of motor-related electroencephalography signals remains challenging in brain-computer interface research. To date, motor imagery of the upper limbs has been extensively investigated, while research on the lower limbs remains limited. Meanwhile, multiple tasks involving the unilateral lower limb (including motor imagery, motor execution, and motor observation for both the left and right lower limb) pose decoding challenges because these tasks activate similar brain regions (i.e., sensorimotor cortex), and contralateral cortex activation is closer to the brain's midline compared to the upper limbs. These challenges make classification challenging for existing deep learning models. To address the above problem, we proposed a collaborative network of bidirectional Mamba and convolutional attention feature selection (CN-BMCAFS) to classify multiple tasks of the unilateral lower limb. In CN-BMCAFS, a global temporal bidirectional Mamba module (GT Bi-Mamba) is employed to capture globally discriminative temporal features. The convolutional attention feature selection module (CAFS) is designed to capture informative local temporal features. The GT Bi-Mamba and CAFS are cascaded in a recurrent manner, enabling the combined advantage of GT Bi-Mamba capturing global temporal features while considering local temporal correlations and CAFS capturing local temporal features while considering global temporal correlations. The results demonstrated that CN-BMCAFS achieved the best performance in classification accuracy, with an accuracy improvement ranging from 1.79% to 14.5% compared to other models. Visualization results show that GT Bi-Mamba enhances the model's ability to accurately distinguish features among MI, ME, and MO, thereby improving decoding performance.

papers.title: Multiscale EEG network alterations in adolescents with depressive symptoms: static-dynamic connectivity, topological features, and exploratory scalp-level network hubs.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for brain network development and a vulnerable stage for the emergence of depressive symptoms Although altered brain connectivity has been reported in depression, the multiscale organization of resting-state EEG networks in adolescents with depressive symptoms (ADS) remains insufficiently understood. In particular, conventional network analyses are often constrained by fixed thresholding strategies and single-level observations, which may obscure scale-specific and topology-related abnormalities. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG data were collected from 96 adolescents with depressive symptoms and 154 healthy controls. A data-driven adaptive thresholding strategy was used to construct subject-specific brain functional networks. Static functional connectivity, dynamic functional connectivity, and higher-order topological features were analyzed across macro-, meso-, and micro-scale levels. A multidimensional abnormality convergence matrix was further constructed to explore the spatial correspondence between network abnormalities and exploratory scalp-level neuromodulation hubs. ADS showed scale-dependent abnormalities in brain network organization. At the macro- and meso-scale levels, abnormalities were mainly characterized by theta-band static hyperconnectivity, particularly involving central-region networks, together with reduced dynamic transition flexibility involving prefrontal systems. Micro-scale analysis further localized these alterations to specific connections and nodes. Static connectivity abnormalities were mainly observed along the midline prefrontal-central axis, including Fp1/Fz-FCz connections, whereas dynamic instability was mainly found in right prefrontal-occipital pathways, including Fp2/F4-Oz connections. Higher-order topological analysis indicated vulnerability of right prefrontal nodes, particularly Fp2 and F4. The convergence matrix showed spatial overlap between abnormal network features and the approximate scalp projections of prefrontal neuromodulation sites, while also identifying FCz and Oz as additional nodes that may warrant further investigation. This study provides a multiscale EEG network characterization of adolescents with depressive symptoms. The findings suggest that ADS-related network alterations may involve coexisting compensatory connectivity changes, reduced dynamic flexibility, and focal topological vulnerability. These results may help refine network-level features and provide hypothesis-generating computational references for future studies exploring individualized neuromodulation strategies in adolescents with depressive symptoms.

papers.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Neurophysiology Alterations in Association with Aβ and Tau Pathology Across the Symptomatic Stages of Alzheimer's Disease Continuum: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau deposition drive Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, how these proteinopathies are linked to macroscopic neural activity alterations measured by electroencephalography (EEG) in symptomatic AD remains inadequately characterized. This study aims to investigate the associations between Aβ, tau, EEG neurophysiology, and cognition. We conducted a cross-sectional study of 73 MCI and AD participants, who underwent resting-state EEG, Aβ-PET, and tau-PET. EEG source analysis was performed to extract regional spectral power. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the associations of regional Aβ (quantified by SUVR), tau (binary classification), with EEG features, controlling for age, sex and education. Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression was applied to investigate the relationships of EEG spectral power and global Aβ burden with cognitive performance. Elevated Aβ burden was associated with distinct regional spectral alterations. Specifically, higher Aβ SUVR was significantly correlated with increased theta power and decreased beta power in a subset of cortical regions. Tau positivity did not modulate the amyloid-theta association in any region, but attenuated the amyloid-beta association in a small set of parietal regions. We identified a localized pattern of Aβ-related neurophysiological dysfunction across the symptomatic stages of AD continuum, characterized by theta increases and beta decreases, supporting a robust association between Aβ burden and cortical neural slowing. The findings highlight the value of source-localized EEG power as a sensitive indicator of Aβ-associated network dysfunction in AD and underscore the potential of source-localized EEG as a complementary, non-invasive biomarker for assessing pathological burden and informing diagnostic strategies in AD.

papers.title: EEG functional connectivity as a prognostic biomarker of adaptive function in autistic people.
papers.abstract: Many autistic people have challenges with adaptive function, impacting education, employment and independent-living goals. Adaptive function outcomes of autistic people vary considerably, which makes planning for future needs challenging. Here, using a developmentally sensitive approach, we investigated if cortico-cortical functional connectivity - a core neurobiological feature that differs in autism - could predict longitudinal changes in adaptive function in autistic people. Using electroencephalography in 150 autistic and 159 non-autistic participants aged 6-31 years, we investigated if mean degree and network organisation (small-world index) predict longitudinal changes in adaptive function over 19-months. We found that small-world index significantly predicted changes in adaptive function in autistic people across the entire age-range. Predictive performance was best for autistic youth (15-24-year-olds), where mean degree and small-world index explained 21 and 30% of additional variance in outcomes, respectively, outperforming measures of intelligence and autistic features. In categorising binary (improved versus not-improved) outcomes, the model containing mean degree had an AUC of 0.84 [95% CI: 0.71-0.97] in 15-24-year-olds, while that containing small-world index had an AUC of 0.76 [95% CI: 0.63-0.89] across the 6-31-year age-range. Both metrics demonstrated properties desired in prognostic biomarkers: high test-retest reliability and convergence with underlying biology (significant associations with genetic variation in brain volume-related genes). Thus, we demonstrate the first evidence that electroencephalography-derived functional connectivity metrics show promise as prognostic biomarkers of adaptive function in autistic people. Potential precision-medicine applications include stratifying participants in clinical trials and identifying those at risk of declining function in clinical settings.

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics of Multi-Item Working Memory Maintenance in Human Gaze Patterns and EEG
papers.abstract: Maintaining multiple items in working memory (WM) requires the allocation of limited resources, which may involve prioritizing individual items over others. Previous work has suggested that attentional prioritization can vary rhythmically between WM samples, but direct empirical evidence for such temporal fluctuations remains scarce. Here, we recorded eye-tracking and EEG to track the temporal dynamics of multi-item processing while participants maintained up to three object orientations in WM. Whereas EEG encoding was only short-lived, miniature gaze patterns reflected the orientations of all three items throughout the entire WM delay and showed systematic load and serial position effects. Contrary to rhythmic sampling accounts, however, we found no evidence that eye movements alternated between the concurrently maintained items. Furthermore, the strength of WM encoding in gaze was not modulated by frontal theta activity in EEG, suggesting that oculomotor encoding was not directly coupled to rhythmic neural dynamics associated with WM and internal attention. Together, our findings indicate that the oculomotor signature of visuospatial WM processing was rather stably shaped by all of the simultaneously maintained items. The results further corroborate that eye-tracking and EEG provide complementary windows into the temporal dynamics of WM.

papers.title: Multimodal synthesis of neural correlates of motor imagery after spinal cord injury: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) profoundly disrupts motor output while also reshaping central motor systems. Motor imagery (MI) provides a valuable window into retained motor-related neural processes because it enables investigation of covert motor state generation in the absence of overt movement. However, evidence on MI after SCI remains fragmented across neurophysiological and neuroimaging modalities. The objective of this review was to systematically synthesize evidence on the neural correlates of MI after SCI across electroencephalography (EEG), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and intracortical recordings. A systematic search of MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, and EBSCOhost was conducted from database inception to March 2026. Original studies were included if they involved individuals with SCI, used an explicit MI task, and reported MI-related neural outcomes derived from EEG, fMRI, MEG, or intracortical recordings. Because of substantial heterogeneity in injury profiles, task paradigms, modalities, and neural outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was performed. Thirty-four studies met the inclusion criteria, including 15 EEG, 10 fMRI, 4 MEG, and 5 intracortical recording studies. Across modalities, MI-related neural activity remained detectable after SCI, with evidence spanning oscillatory responses, regional recruitment, network organization, and fine-grained neural representations. Many studies also described altered recruitment patterns, modified connectivity, atypical task-related modulation, or changes in representational structure. Findings varied according to injury phenotype, chronicity, task design, and analytical framework. The four modalities provided complementary evidence on post-SCI motor imagery across temporal, spatial, network, and neuronal scales. Available evidence indicates that MI-related neural activity is generally detectable after SCI, although its organization is often altered. A multimodal perspective is therefore necessary for understanding both the persistence and the reshaping of motor representations after injury. These findings support continued investigation of MI in neurorehabilitation and neurotechnology, while also highlighting the need for approaches that account for post-injury heterogeneity.

papers.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
papers.abstract: Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

papers.title: Beyond Exploration: Heightened Recent Reward Reliance and Midfrontal Sensitivity to Outcome Differences in ADHD
papers.abstract: Adaptive decision-making requires balancing the exploitation of known rewards with the exploration of alternative options, yet how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) shapes this trade-off remains unclear. Using a restless four-armed bandit task and electroencephalography (EEG), we investigated the neural correlates of exploratory decisions and how recent rewards shape choice behavior and feedback processing in 23 adults with self-reported clinical ADHD diagnoses and 27 controls. Across 450 trials with dynamically changing payoffs, choices were classified against the highest last-observed payoff, and behavioral modeling quantified the influence of reward history on subsequent decisions. Contrary to our predictions, exploration rates, task performance, and neural differentiation between exploration and exploitation did not differ significantly between groups. However, adults with ADHD were more likely to repeat an option after high reward feedback and switch after low rewards, driven primarily by the immediately preceding outcome. At neural level, ADHD participants also showed greater midfrontal sensitivity to unsigned changes between consecutive payoffs, expressed in a feedback-evoked response spanning 280 to 568 ms and carried by slow activity below 2 Hz. Together, these findings dissociate the raw frequency of exploration from the dynamic weighting of recent outcomes in ADHD. Rather than reflecting an indiscriminate drive for novelty, behavior was characterized by heightened recent reward reliance paired with amplified slow-wave midfrontal sensitivity to outcome shifts. Crucially, this profile emerged without compromising overall performance, suggesting that, in this volatile environment, ADHD was associated with an increased weighting of recent outcomes rather than with a performance deficit.

papers.title: Comb-Like EEG Pattern as an Early Diagnostic Clue in Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a life-threatening inborn error of amino acid metabolism that often presents in the neonatal period with nonspecific symptoms such as poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures. Although newborn screening (NBS) enables early identification, false-negative results and delays in reporting may lead to missed or delayed diagnosis, resulting in severe neurologic injury. A characteristic EEG finding, the "comb-like rhythm," consisting of central- or frontocentral-predominant, sharply contoured 4-7 Hz theta bursts has been reported in MSUD. However, its diagnostic utility has not been systematically evaluated. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the comb-like rhythm as a diagnostic clue for MSUD. A systematic literature search was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines using MEDLINE and Embase databases up to May 18, 2026. Studies evaluating EEG findings in individuals with MSUD were included. Data on clinical presentation, biochemical findings, brain imaging, and EEG features were extracted and synthesized qualitatively. In addition, two neonatal cases from our institution were included. Associations of the comb-like EEG rhythm with patient age at EEG (neonatal vs. non-neonatal) and plasma leucine concentrations were evaluated using Fisher's exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test. A total of 113 records were screened, and 18 studies were included, comprising 24 symptomatic cases including our two patients. Abnormal EEG findings were reported in 21 of 24 (88%). A comb-like pattern was exclusively observed in neonates with acute metabolic crisis (13/15 neonates [86.7%] vs. 0/9 non-neonates [0%], p < 0.0001). The comb-like rhythm was associated with higher plasma leucine concentrations (median, 3545 vs. 1782 μmol/L, p = 0.0033). The pattern often diminished or resolved following treatment or clinical stabilization. In our two patients, the comb-like rhythm contributed to raising diagnostic suspicion despite initially normal NBS results. The comb-like rhythm may serve as an adjunctive EEG marker that raises suspicion for acute MSUD, given its strong association with neonatal metabolic crisis and severe hyperleucinemia. Further studies are needed to clarify its pathophysiological basis and determine the clinical utility of EEG in MSUD crisis.

papers.title: Effects of Pore Mutations on 1/f Flicker Noise Reveal Differences in CFTR Substates.
papers.abstract: Many disease-causing mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR), a key chloride channel, lead to cystic fibrosis by disrupting the regulation and stability of its different open and closed substates. These transitions generate rapid current fluctuations observed in patch-clamp measurements, known as flicker noise, which can reveal information about chloride flow and state dynamics in the wild type and different mutants. Using time-frequency analysis with spectrograms applied to single-channel recordings, we found that the power of higher-frequency components (10-1000 Hz) was greater during the open state than during the closed state. Frequency analysis showed 1fα noise in the fully open state (α = 0.5) and a flat power spectral density (PSD) in the closed state (α = 0). Using several pore mutants as representations of the three open states (S1, S2, and F), we found that the S2 frequency signature was similar to the fully open state (α = 0.5), whereas S1 behaved more similarly to the closed state (α = 0) in terms of flicker noise. A mutant affecting the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) did not show changes in α. These frequency signatures were not altered by changes in electrochemical forces in the WT and may be linked to conformational changes and differences in the energy landscape and trapping of Chloride ions in energy wells during the permeation process. Using the Hurst exponent, derived from spectral analysis, we showed that S1 exhibited memoryless dynamics (H ≈ 0.5), while S2 and F showed persistent behavior (H > 0.5), indicating that memory structure depends on the substate. These experimental findings were reproduced using a transistor-based model that incorporates flicker noise and maps electrophysiological variables (τo, τc, Po, α) to circuit parameters. This allows linking functional CFTR states (C0, C1, C2, S1, S2, F) to electronic components, enabling fast, variant-specific simulations.

papers.title: Fast-Gelling, Adhesive, and Conductive Epidermal Electrode for Accurate Physiological Signal Monitoring and Real-Time Brain-Controlled Drone Flight.
papers.abstract: Conductive hydrogel electrodes are vital components for achieving human-machine interfaces. However, the inherent trade-off between high conductivity and favorable mechanical/adhesive properties remains a significant challenge for hydrogel-based epidermal electrodes. Here, we developed a multifunctional MXene/WPU/PAA (MWA) hydrogel electrode that combines robust mechanical properties, strong adhesion, and excellent conductivity. The introduced MXene nanosheets can induce free-radical polymerization, resulting in fast gelation (<5 min) at room temperature. Theoretical analyses reveal that MXene nanosheets form abundant hydrogen bonds with polymer chains, thus enhancing the cross-linking density and mechanical strength of the hydrogel electrode. The MWA hydrogel can form a stable skin-electrode interface, enabling high-fidelity multimodal physiological signal monitoring. Specifically, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for sEMG reached 36.0 dB, while the SNR for ECG was 30.1 dB, outperforming the Ag/AgCl electrodes. The MWA hydrogel exhibits outstanding adhesion under repeated cycles and simulated sweat conditions, reaching 94.2 and 55.5 kPa, respectively. Furthermore, the MWA hydrogel electrode demonstrates precise scalp EEG monitoring, enabling wireless drone flight control via real-time brainwave decoding. This work provides insight into MXene-polymer interactions and demonstrates the applicability of the developed electrode to brain-computer interface applications.

papers.title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology
papers.abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

papers.title: Psychosis of Epilepsy: A Review of Diagnosis and Management.
papers.abstract: Neurology and psychiatry have been linked together for a long period of time. One overlap demonstrated in the literature is the correlation between epilepsy with mood and psychosis. There is a big group of psychoses called the psychosis of epilepsy (POE); however, there is not much evidence about the diagnosis and management. Differentiation between POEs is difficult and is compounded by a lack of evidence-based guidelines on appropriate management. Even if you arrive at the diagnosis, POE can be difficult to manage. Some antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) cause psychiatric side effects and some antipsychotics may be epileptogenic. In this poster, we will discuss ways to diagnose and treat POE, as well as how to optimize certain AEDs in patients with POE. Articles were chosen from multiple databases, such as MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and PsychInfo, to gather evidence about the diagnosis and management of POE. Specific keywords, such as Psychosis, Epilepsy, Antipsychotic, Antiepileptic, and Electroencephalogram (EEG) were used. Articles talking about recommendations regarding the use of AEDs and antipsychotics in POE were extracted from these databases. POE includes preictal, ictal, postictal, and interictal psychosis. Preictal psychosis is very rare and tends to present with dissociation and déjà vu. This is correlated with temporal lobe epilepsy and resolves after the seizure. Ictal psychosis will correspond with epileptic activity on EEG and can manifest as aggression, delusions, or hallucinations. Antipsychotics are contraindicated in this POE. Postictal psychosis usually presents as a combination of mood symptoms and grandiose delusions seen with interictal sharp epileptiform discharges on EEG. Interictal psychosis can be subtyped into brief and chronic, with brief occurring during periods of increasing seizure frequency and chronic having no association with seizures. They both present similar to symptoms seen in classic schizophrenia and antipsychotics are often utilized.Clozapine and chlorpromazine were found to have the highest seizure prevalence from second- and first-generation antipsychotics respectively, and the lowest was found with risperidone. AEDs that are commonly used in psychiatry, such as oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, valproic acid, and lamotrigine are discussed in detail regarding their optimal dosing strategy for patients presenting with POE. Diagnosis and management of the various types of POE can be challenging due to the lack of literature. We recommend using the antipsychotic, risperidone, as it has shown to have the lowest seizure prevalence among all antipsychotics. Both neurologists and psychiatrists should keep POE on their differential when dealing with seizure patients with psychosis. It is crucial for psychiatrists to understand how to optimize AEDs in the management of POE as these patients are often seen on the consult service. No Funding.

papers.title: Aphasic status epilepticus presenting with prominent psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
papers.abstract: Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is a subtype of nonconvulsive status epilepticus characterized by aphasia as its primary ictal manifestation. Although psychiatric symptoms are uncommon in ASE, they may obscure the diagnosis when present. We report an atypical case, presenting predominantly with agitation and irritability, which was rapidly diagnosed as ASE by electroencephalography (EEG) based on the abrupt symptom onset and neurological history. A 49-year-old right-handed woman with alcohol use disorder was referred to our psychiatric hospital because of agitation, irritability, and disorganized thinking. Approximately 2 months before presentation to our hospital, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days after sustaining a head injury. A left posterior fossa subdural hematoma was diagnosed, and burr-hole evacuation was performed at a general hospital. She continued rehabilitation; however, 6 days before admission to our hospital, she suddenly developed incoherent speech with agitation and irritability, prompting referral to our psychiatric hospital. Neurological examination revealed sensory aphasia. Given the history of brain injury and abrupt symptom onset, EEG was performed and demonstrated left-dominant periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, confirming ASE. Antiseizure treatment resolved the EEG abnormalities and aphasia; however, aphasia, agitation, and irritability recurred with periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. The symptoms improved with intravenous diazepam, and no recurrence was observed for >2 years following optimization of antiseizure medication. ASE may present predominantly with psychiatric symptoms and be misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Recognizing symptom chronology and epileptogenic background is essential for prompting EEG evaluation and early diagnosis.

papers.title: Effect of neurofeedback-assisted mindfulness training on migraine severity, associated disability, sleep quality, and emotional distress: protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Migraine is a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a leading cause of worldwide disability, exerting significant clinical, social, and economic burdens. While pharmacological options exist, their efficacy is often limited by tolerability issues and risk of medication-overuse headache. Neurofeedback (NF) combined with mindfulness training has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological neuromodulation technique. However, clinical evidence in migraine management remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and small sample sizes. This study protocol aims to evaluate the efficacy of a Neurofeedback-Assisted Mindfulness Training Program (NAMTP) in adults with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine. This is a randomized, parallel-group, controlled clinical trial protocol. Sixty-six (N = 66) adults diagnosed with medium-to-high-frequency episodic migraine (5-14 monthly migraine days) will be recruited and randomized (1:1 ratio) into either the Intervention Group (IG: standard care plus NAMTP) or the Control Group (CG: standard routine care alone). The IG will undergo a 12-week home-based program consisting of 60 sessions (15-20 min each, 5 times per week) of mindfulness training assisted by the Muse® electroencephalography (EEG) headband. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, 12 weeks (post-intervention), and 24 weeks post-randomization. The powered primary outcome is the change in Monthly Migraine Days (MMDs). Secondary outcomes include migraine-associated disability (MIDAS), headache impact (HIT-6), sleep parameters (actigraphy and PSQI), quality of life (MSQ v.2), and mood symptoms (BDI-II and STAI-Y). This protocol addresses the urgent need for scalable, non-pharmacological therapies in migraine management. By combining objective neurophysiological monitoring with behavioral training within a rigorous randomized controlled framework, this trial will clarify whether NAMTP can reduce headache burden, optimize sleep patterns, and diminish affective distress. The findings are expected to provide standardized, actionable evidence regarding the integration of digital neurofeedback tools into routine clinical care for episodic migraine.Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07661888.

papers.title: Side-to-side and other complex head movements as ictal signs in epilepsy: A video-EEG case series and review of literature.
papers.abstract: Side-to-side head shaking is often considered a distinctive clinical sign that differentiates functional seizures from epileptic seizures; however, it may also occur as an ictal phenomenon in focal epilepsy. We retrospectively reviewed all video-telemetry reports of patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy undergoing presurgical evaluation between 2015 and 2025. All reports were electronically screened for mentioning side-to-side or other complex head movements and the video-EEG of these patients was reviewed and included if associated with ictal EEG changes. Seventeen patients were identified who experienced 631 seizures in total, 201 of which included such movements (median: 2 per patient, range: 1-160). One patient (No. 5) accounted for 79% of these events and represented an outlier. Head movements were predominantly horizontal (93.5%), followed by mixed (5%) and rotatory (1.5%). While small-amplitude movements predominated overall, larger amplitudes were more frequent after excluding the outlier case. In six patients, head movements were the initial observed feature of seizure semiology and typically represented a brief component of the seizure, although prolonged in the outlier case. Interrater agreement ranged from fair to good across semiological variables. Presumed epileptogenic zones were heterogenous, including frontal, temporal, anterior quadrant, and hemispheric regions. Ictal side-to-side and other complex head movements can occur in focal epilepsies but lack localizing or lateralizing value. They likely reflect seizure propagation and involvement of broader neuronal circuits. Further studies are needed to clarify their mechanisms and clinical significance.

papers.title: Ethical Risks and Governance of Consumer Electroencephalography-Based Neurotechnology: Qualitative Interview Study With Expert Stakeholders
papers.abstract: Background Consumer electroencephalography (EEG)-based neurotechnologies are rapidly expanding across commercial digital health delivery networks and wellness markets. Positioned at the intersection of non-medical self-monitoring and clinical applications, these consumer devices introduce complex challenges for device governance and digital bioethics regarding product claims, data privacy, evidential substantiation, and user protection. Objective This qualitative study examined expert stakeholder perspectives on the ethical, regulatory, and data governance challenges of consumer EEG neurotechnology, focusing on the allocation of responsibility across product lifecycles. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 expert stakeholders spanning research, clinical practice, engineering, industry, ethics, law, and regulatory policy across North America, Europe, and Latin America. Interview data were systematically analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to examine how governance challenges, evidence burdens, and responsibilities are conceptualized across the neurotechnology ecosystem. Results Five interrelated themes emerged: (1) Regulatory Category Boundaries and Oversight; (2) Evidential Credibility and Claims-Related Harm; (3) Neurodata Privacy, Security, and Inference; (4) Layered Governance and Explicit Accountability; and (5) Participation, Global Equity, and Contextual Responsiveness. Participants identified major friction in applying traditional medical oversight to nonmedical digital health uses, linked unverified claims to user vulnerability, and expressed concern over downstream neurodata processing. A connecting synthesis demonstrates that oversight responsibilities span multiple actors and development stages rather than resting on a single regulatory mechanism. Conclusions Effective governance of consumer EEG digital health devices requires explicit allocation of duties for claims substantiation, data practices, and user safety, backed by inclusive stakeholder participation and contextual responsiveness.
