papers.title: From attention capture to responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI discrimination crises.
papers.abstract: Understanding how publics respond to discrimination by artificial intelligence (AI) matters for organizations managing technology-related crises. Using the associative-propositional evaluation (APE) model as an organizing framework, this study reports two experiments comparing AI discrimination with executive discrimination. Study 1 (N = 148) used a controlled news scenario. AI discrimination produced higher corporate responsibility attribution, whereas executive discrimination produced lower corporate reputation and higher negative word-of-mouth (NWOM) intention; because the NWOM scale was only moderately reliable (α = 0.54, ω = 0.55), that result is reported as preliminary. Study 2 (N = 30) used electroencephalography (EEG) while participants viewed simulated social-media messages. AI discrimination elicited a larger P2 amplitude (dz = 0.60) and lower frontal-central theta-band activity (dz = -0.43) than executive discrimination, whereas the behavioral responsibility-attribution difference was small and not statistically significant (dz = 0.32, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.68]). Read together, the two studies show a separation between responsibility judgment and punishment-related responses: under the same actor cue, responsibility rose while punishment-related responses moved in the opposite direction, and the cue was registered within the first quarter-second of processing. This pattern constrains dual-process accounts of crisis response. The findings may inform, rather than prescribe, organizational communication and governance responses to discrimination crises.

papers.title: Machine learning framework to enhance and automate cardiovascular outpatient triage for patients with atrial fibrillation.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia, placing a substantial burden on the healthcare system. Patients with AF are cared for in a variety of settings, including primary care and cardiovascular (CV) clinics, while some require cardiac electrophysiology (EP) clinics that offer specialized drugs or procedures. Triage of AF referrals to these specific clinics will lead to timely and proper care and reduce inefficiency in the health system. The goal is to develop a machine learning framework to triage the likelihood of patient referrals to EP-directed treatments. We retrospectively analyzed 6,755 patients who were referred to CV with a referral diagnosis of AF. Data encompassed patient demographics, relevant comorbidities, medications, prior procedures, medical notes analyzed using natural language processing (NLP), and Holter monitoring data. A two-stage framework, predicting the necessity for specialized EP care, was developed: the construction of the machine learning model, followed by post-refinement based on established clinical criteria. The Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) model emerged as the most effective model in the first stage, achieving an area under the curve of 0.77, an accuracy of 72%, a true positive rate (TPR) of 67%, and a false positive rate of 23%. The post-refinement stage further improved TPR to as much as 83%. This framework resulted in increased identification of EP-direct patient care from the current reported 20% to 46%. Our framework effectively identifies patients who are likely to require specialized EP care, thereby enhancing the automation of the AF referral triage process and potentially improving efficiency.

papers.title: Potential Applications of Brain-Computer Interface Technology in the Rehabilitation of Patients with Anxiety Disorders: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent mental disorders worldwide and can cause persistent impairment in emotional regulation, cognition, and social functioning. Pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, exercise, and non-invasive brain stimulation are widely used, yet their effectiveness may be constrained by dependence liability, interindividual variability, treatment engagement, incomplete response, and limited objective measures of treatment processes. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) acquire, decode, and feed back neural signals-most commonly electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), or real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (rt-fMRI)-thereby converting anxiety-related brain activity into targets that can be monitored, trained, or used to trigger intervention. This narrative review examines the mechanistic rationale for BCI-assisted anxiety rehabilitation, technological approaches across levels of invasiveness, and integration with pharmacological, psychological, and exercise-based care. Current evidence indicates that EEG has been used for both anxiety-state recognition and neurofeedback; rt-fMRI enables targeted modulation of deep emotion-related networks and functional connectivity; and fNIRS offers promise for portable prefrontal monitoring and as an input signal for closed-loop systems. Invasive closed-loop systems can directly record from and stimulate local or deep circuits, but anxiety-related evidence is derived mainly from animal studies, patients undergoing intracranial monitoring, and neurological populations with comorbid anxiety, and therefore demonstrates technical feasibility rather than efficacy in primary anxiety disorders. Overall, BCIs are better positioned as potential adjuncts to established care than as replacements. The field remains limited by small, single-center studies, inadequate follow-up, heterogeneous acquisition and training protocols, and unresolved governance of neural data. Because this is a narrative review without a formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis, its conclusions should be regarded as exploratory. Multicenter randomized controlled trials, harmonized technical and reporting standards, cross-device external validation, and risk-proportionate ethical and regulatory frameworks are needed to determine whether BCIs can be translated from proof of concept into safe, effective, and implementable tools for anxiety rehabilitation.

papers.title: Visualization of super-selective Wada with computed tomography perfusion: toward a novel option in preoperative functional mapping.
papers.abstract: The Wada test has long been a well-established method for evaluating hemispheric dominance and functional localization; however, it has not been established as a visualizable functional imaging modality. Recently, the super-selective Wada test (ssWada) has emerged as a technique enabling more localized functional evaluation. By selectively catheterizing distal cerebral arterial branches, ssWada enables territory-based functional evaluation with higher spatial resolution than conventional approaches. In this study, we combined ssWada with computed tomography perfusion (CTP) to visualize pharmacologically inactivated brain regions preoperatively. These data were further fused with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and CT to propose a novel functional mapping approach delineating the relationship between perfusion-defined functional territories, lesions, and seizure onset zone (SOZ)-related stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) contacts. Patients who underwent ssWada for preoperative evaluation of brain tumors or drug-resistant epilepsy at our institution were included. During ssWada, propofol was selectively injected via a microcatheter into the ICA and distal branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), as well as the anterior or posterior cerebral artery when necessary. Perfusion territories were simultaneously visualized using CTP. These datasets were subsequently fused with MRI and post-SEEG CT to evaluate the spatial relationship between perfusion-defined functional territories, lesions, and SOZ-related SEEG contacts. Among the 23 patients, hemispheric dominance was left in 18 patients (78.3%), bilateral in 3 (13.0%), and right in 2 (8.7%). No complications were observed. In the MCA superior trunk territory, repetition, naming, and reading tasks showed positive rates of approximately 70%. In contrast, in the inferior trunk territory, repetition and reading demonstrated high positive rates (93.8%), whereas naming positivity was lower (56.3%). Fusion with MRI and post-SEEG CT enabled spatial visualization of lesions and SOZ-related SEEG contacts within perfusion-defined functional territories, facilitating individualized functional-anatomical assessment for surgical planning. ssWada combined with CTP enables territory-based visualization of pharmacologically inactivated brain regions and provides a novel preoperative functional mapping approach with high spatial resolution. Fusion with MRI and post-SEEG CT further facilitates individualized functional-anatomical assessment of lesions and SOZ-related networks. These findings support the clinical utility of ssWada-CTP fusion imaging as a novel strategy for individualized preoperative functional brain mapping.
